body.statement: Suppose \(m\) is odd and no allowed edge \(j\to i\) has \(A_{ii}=A_{jj}=0\). Then every nonempty \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) is a singleton. Its diagonal is \(A_{ii}=B_{ii}^{1/m}\); its allowed off-diagonal entries are recovered in increasing endpoint gap by \(A_{ij}=\{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)\}/C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})\); and its diagonal innovations are recovered in increasing \(i\) by \(D_{ii}=\{Q_{ii}-\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^2\}/\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}\). For arbitrary \((B,Q)\), the recursively produced candidate is compatible if and only if its diagonal is stable, every recovered \(D_{ii}\) is positive, every forbidden entry of \(A^m=B\) holds, and the complete covariance equation \(Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top\) holds. Consequently every nonempty compatible transfer fiber satisfies \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)=\{h_{uv}\}\).
body.justification: This theorem retains the stronger full-parameter singleton result under noncollision on every allowed edge; the new target-corridor theorem shows that full uniqueness is unnecessary for the causal transfer.
body.gap: Classical triangular-root recursion computes a chosen root but does not prove graph- and covariance-compatible uniqueness, while Gong et al.'s positive theorem uses a different non-Gaussian information regime.
body.consumer: Users needing the entire fine transition and diagonal innovation covariance may apply the global recursion; transfer-only users can invoke the weaker corridor theorem.
body.proof_tex:
Let \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\), the matrix \(A\) is lower triangular, it obeys the graph-support zero restrictions, \(\max_i|A_{ii}|<1\), the matrix \(D\) is diagonal with \(D_{ii}>0\), and
\[
 A^m=B,
 \qquad
 Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top .
\]

We first identify the diagonal of \(A\).  Multiplication of lower-triangular matrices shows that the \((i,i)\) entry of a product is the product of the \((i,i)\) entries.  Induction on \(r\) therefore gives
\[
 (A^r)_{ii}=A_{ii}^r,
 \qquad
 B_{ii}=(A^m)_{ii}=A_{ii}^m.
\]
By \(\mathrm{ass{:}odd\mbox{-}factor}\), \(m\) is odd.  For real \(x<y\),
\[
 y^m-x^m=(y-x)\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}y^{m-1-k}x^k>0;
\]
indeed, if \(x\) and \(y\) have the same sign this is immediate after factoring their absolute values, while if \(x<0<y\), then \(x^m<0<y^m\).  Thus \(x\mapsto x^m\) is injective on \(\mathbb R\), and every compatible pair must have the same diagonal
\[
 A_{ii}=B_{ii}^{1/m},
\]
where the right side denotes the unique real odd root.

We next recover the strict lower triangle by induction on the endpoint gap \(g=i-j\).  Suppose that all entries whose gaps are smaller than \(g\) have already been fixed.  If \(j\to i\) is allowed by \(G\), the result \(\mathrm{lem{:}path\mbox{-}expansion}\) gives
\[
 B_{ij}=A_{ij}C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})+R_{ij,m}(A).
\]
Every off-diagonal factor appearing in the remainder has endpoint gap strictly less than \(g\), so the induction hypothesis and the graph-support zeros determine \(R_{ij,m}(A)\).  The theorem's noncollision premise says that \((A_{ii},A_{jj})\ne(0,0)\) on every allowed edge.  The odd part of \(\mathrm{lem{:}divided\mbox{-}difference\mbox{-}zero\mbox{-}set}\) consequently yields
\[
 C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})>0.
\]
Division is valid and forces
\[
 A_{ij}=\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)}{C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})}.
\]
If \(j\to i\) is not allowed, \(\mathrm{ass{:}graph\mbox{-}support}\) instead forces \(A_{ij}=0\); and \(\mathrm{ass{:}lower\mbox{-}triangular}\) forces \(A_{ij}=0\) when \(i<j\).  Starting with \(g=1\) and continuing through \(g=d-1\) therefore determines every entry of \(A\).  In particular, two elements of the compatible fiber have the same transition matrix.

Fix this uniquely determined \(A\).  Because \(D\) is diagonal, the \((i,i)\) coordinate of the covariance equation is
\[
 Q_{ii}
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{d}(A^r)_{ij}D_{jj}(A^r)_{ij}
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{d}D_{jj}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}.
\]
Every power of a lower-triangular matrix is lower triangular, so \((A^r)_{ij}=0\) for \(j>i\), and the diagonal identity above gives \((A^r)_{ii}=A_{ii}^r\).  Hence
\[
 Q_{ii}
 =D_{ii}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}
  +\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}.
\]
The coefficient
\[
 s_i:=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}
\]
is at least its \(r=0\) summand, namely one.  Induction over \(i=1,\ldots,d\) therefore permits division by \(s_i\) and uniquely gives
\[
 D_{ii}
 =\frac{Q_{ii}-\displaystyle\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}
                 \displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}}
        {\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}}.
\]
Thus two members of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) also have the same \(D\), proving that a nonempty compatible fiber is a singleton.

It remains to prove the claimed exact compatibility test, including sufficiency.  For an input satisfying the theorem's odd-root noncollision condition, construct a candidate \(A^\star\) by the displayed diagonal and allowed-edge recursions, set all structurally forbidden coordinates to zero, and then construct diagonal \(D^\star\) by the covariance recursion.  The diagonal equations \(((A^\star)^m)_{ii}=B_{ii}\) hold by the odd-root construction.  On each allowed edge, the path-expansion identity and the defining recursion give \(((A^\star)^m)_{ij}=B_{ij}\).  Therefore \((A^\star)^m=B\) holds exactly when it also holds at every remaining, structurally forbidden coordinate.  The diagonal covariance equations hold by construction, and the full covariance check is exactly
\[
 Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^\star)^rD^\star((A^\star)^r)^\top.
\]
The matrix \(A^\star\) has the required triangular and graph zeros by construction.  Its stability condition in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) is exactly \(\max_i|A^\star_{ii}|<1\).  Since \(D^\star\) is diagonal, \(D^\star\succ0\) is equivalent to \(D^\star_{ii}>0\) for every \(i\).  Consequently the stability check, positivity of every recovered innovation variance, the remaining coordinates of \((A^\star)^m=B\), and the complete covariance equation together imply every condition in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\), and hence are sufficient.  Conversely, if a compatible pair exists, the preceding uniqueness argument shows that it equals \((A^\star,D^\star)\); the definition of the fiber then makes every listed check necessary.  This proves the stated if-and-only-if criterion for the recursively produced candidate.

Finally, \(\mathrm{def{:}transfer\mbox{-}fiber}\) maps each compatible structural pair to the direct structural transfer
\[
 z\longmapsto \frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}.
\]
This is the causal target specified by the fine-grid structural equation, whereas \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is its observed-law compatible image.  For \(|z|=1\), stability implies \(|A_{vv}z|=|A_{vv}|<1\), so the denominator is nonzero.  Since the compatible parameter fiber is a singleton, its image is the singleton \(\{h_{uv}\}\).  Thus the causal transfer is identified from \((B,Q,G,m)\), rather than being equated to an observed-law functional by definition.

For an exact regular stress test, take \(d=2\), \(m=3\), let \(G\) contain \(1\to2\), and set
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\[2pt]1/4&1/3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad D=I_2.
\]
Both endpoint persistences are nonzero and \(A\) is stable.  There is no indirect path, and direct multiplication, equivalently the path expansion, gives
\[
 B_{11}=\frac18,
 \qquad B_{22}=\frac1{27},
 \qquad B_{21}=\frac14 C_3\!\left(\frac13,\frac12\right)
 =\frac14\left(\frac19+\frac16+\frac14\right)
 =\frac{19}{144}.
\]
Since \(C_3(1/3,1/2)=19/36\), the recursion returns \(A_{21}=1/4\).  For the generated coarse covariance, direct calculation gives
\[
 Q_{11}=\frac{21}{16},
 \qquad
 Q_{22}=\frac{61}{576}+\frac{91}{81}.
\]
The innovation recursion consequently returns
\[
 D_{11}=\frac{21/16}{1+1/4+1/16}=1,
 \qquad
 D_{22}=\frac{Q_{22}-(1/16+25/576)}{1+1/9+1/81}=1.
\]
Thus it recovers the transfer \(z/[4(1-z/3)]\).

The noncollision condition is load-bearing.  Keep \(d=2\), \(m=3\), and the same allowed edge, and for \(q_1,q_2>0\) define
\[
 A(a)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ a&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 D(a)=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2-a^2q_1),
 \qquad
 |a|<\sqrt{q_2/q_1}.
\]
Then \(D(a)\succ0\), \(A(a)^2=0\), and hence
\[
 A(a)^3=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{r=0}^{2}A(a)^rD(a)(A(a)^r)^\top
 =D(a)+A(a)D(a)A(a)^\top
 =\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2).
\]
All these stable Gaussian fine-grid models therefore induce the same pair \((B,Q)=(0,\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2))\), but their transfers are \(h_{12}(z)=az\), an open interval of distinct functions.  Here both endpoint persistences vanish and \(C_3(0,0)=0\), so this example violates precisely the noncollision premise used for division and shows why that premise cannot be dropped from the singleton conclusion.
